items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Pops Foster had a certain tape he used to keep from getting them blisters and them pus in your fingers... The same thing was happening with Pops Foster with Luis Russell.

ctx.x: You had a lot of associations with New Orleans musicians up there.

There weren’t that many. The ones who were there, they were working with bands. I was the only one out there by myself. All the musicians was mad about New Orleans musicians, because they were innovators. Al Morgan come in. The first day he was there. Next day he was with the McKinney’s Cotton Pickers. From McKinney’s Cotton Pickers he went with Cab Calloway. All that in three months, because he played bass. They had never heard no bass player like that. They just were beginning to play the bass in 1930, because…

there was the Savoy. Then there was the Renaissance. Aw man, and there was a dozen others places with every element of black people. You get a chance to see all them people. West End the people hang out in one . . . certain bars. The black Cubans hang out in another bar. The Barbadans hang out in another. People from Virginia hang out in another bar. They had all that. People went to the source of their pleasures and their relations. What was that first question?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Lionel Tapo was Big Belly Fob’s nephew.

ctx.x: Lionel Tapo was Big Belly Fob’s nephew. Lionel Tapo. His stepbrother played guitar. Can’t think of his name. You got him there? Lionel and his brother?
His brother-in-law. You mentioned Howard Mandolf.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Pops Foster was with Luis Russell, and everybody was taking lessons from him.

ctx.x: Those are the ones that migrated to Chicago, migrated from New Orleans around 1915, '16 and '17, and migrated from Chicago to Frisco and Oakland and San Diego. Jelly Roll and all of them went out there, when Watts was... They speak of Watts as a cowboy place, a country...you know, Western town.
That almost makes me the oldest one now standing. After you get past Garland and Pops Foster. I guess you ...(?)... and your day will come. There it is. You have to look at Bill Johnson...
